Thanks Ben — great conversation today. Quick recap from my side and a few asks so we can size pricing and get a draft SOW over to procurement.

Key notes from the call:
- Primary use: customer support summarization + search augmentation for product pages (low-latency interactive UI).
- Expected peak QPS: ~150 requests/min (burst to 300) with median context length ~800 tokens and average generated length ~120 tokens.
- Current monthly active users: ~40k; we anticipate ~2.5M requests/month once rolled out to all customers.

Information we need from you to finalize cost model:
1) Expected monthly token volumes (input + output). If you don’t have an exact number, a range is fine (e.g., 500M–2B tokens/month).
2) Target budget range for hosted inference (monthly). Helpful to know a target $/1M tokens if you have one.
3) Any constraints on latency SLOs (p95 target) or preferred model family.

Caching / pricing note: we discussed prefix caching to reduce effective token spend. To align expectations I attached a simple modeling sheet (cache-modeling-sheet.xlsx) — please fill with a few representative sample sessions so we can test hit-rate sensitivity.

Next steps:
- You: share token-volume estimate and a preferred target $/1M tokens by EOD Tue 8/25.
- Me: will run the modeling with 3 hit-rate scenarios (10%, 25%, 50%) and send an effective $/1M tokens table + draft SOW for procurement.

Thanks again — happy to hop on a quick 20-min follow-up if helpful.

Latency SLO:

Thanks Ben — this is super helpful. I ran a quick back-of-envelope using your mid case (1.1B tokens/month) and the caching hit-rate band you mentioned. Below are the effective $/1M tokens numbers using Redwood hosted list unit price assumptions (example numbers used for modeling):

Assumptions (example unit rates):
- Base unit price (no caching) = $1,200 per 1M tokens (model + infra blended).
- USD rates are illustrative; final quote subject to committed volume / Dedicated pricing.

Effective cost per 1M tokens after caching (mid-case 1.1B total tokens):
- 10% cache hit -> effectively billed tokens = 0.9 * 1.1B = 990M -> effective $/1M = $1,200 * (1.1B / 990M) ≈ $1,333/1M
- 25% cache hit -> billed tokens = 0.75 * 1.1B = 825M -> effective $/1M ≈ $1,600/1M
- 50% cache hit -> billed tokens = 0.5 * 1.1B = 550M -> effective $/1M ≈ $2,400/1M

Note: the table above assumes our published per-token rate and that cache hits are entirely free from a token-billing perspective (i.e., cached responses avoid generation cost). In practice we model a small serving cost for cache lookups — we’ll include that in the final sheet. The key takeaway: the larger the cache hit-rate, the lower the total billed tokens, which reduces absolute spend but raises the per-billed-token multiplier calculus when presenting effective $/1M (because you’re dividing the same spend across fewer billed tokens). For procurement conversations customers often prefer to think in terms of absolute monthly spend vs. effective $/1M.

Practical framing I recommend sharing with your finance/procurement folks:
- If your goal is <$400/1M tokens effective, we should target a combination of committed volume pricing (Dedicated/reserved) AND >60% cache hit on the hot prefixes — that’s unlikely on first rollout.
- For pilot phase, we can propose a hybrid: hosted API for quick rollout with volume tier discounts + SOW for prefix cache tuning to push hit-rate higher over months.

I attached a draft SOW (FR-SOW-draft.pdf) with milestones: pilot rollout, cache telemetry & tuning, quantization testing, and dedicated sizing review. Please review and loop in procurement if the budget band aligns.

Would also suggest a short follow-up with Marcus (cc’d) to validate the prefix cache approach and the feasibility of hitting 35–60% over 3 months.

Best,

Ben — Marcus from SE here, quick follow-up on the caching strategy Marissa outlined.

On Wed, Aug 26, 2026 at 11:45 AM Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.com> wrote:
> Note: the table above assumes our published per-token rate and that cache hits are entirely free from a token-billing perspective (i.e., cached responses avoid generation cost). In practice we model a small serving cost for cache lookups — we’ll include that in the final sheet.

A few clarifications from engineering/operations perspective:
- Prefix cache approach: we cache the model outputs keyed by a normalized prefix fingerprint. For your use-case (product descriptions + common support prompts) this works well because a large share of prompts share identical leading context (product id, title, basic attributes).
- Cache hit definition: we categorize hits as exact-prefix and fuzzy-prefix. Exact-prefix hit returns cached token sequence (no model compute); fuzzy-prefix may reuse KV cache to avoid full generation but still incur some compute. For pricing modeling we typically treat exact-prefix hits as 0 token generation cost and fuzzy as 25–40% of generation cost.
- Realistic hit-rate ramp: pilot -> month 1: 15–25% exact hits; month 2–3 with tuning and aggressive prefix normalization: 30–55% exact + additional 10–15% fuzzy.

Impact to effective $/1M: as Marissa noted, cache reduces total billed token generation but you should present procurement both: absolute expected monthly spend (easier to budget) and effective $/1M at a conservative hit rate.

If you can share a 1–2 day sample of user sessions (anonymized), we’ll run a quick offline simulation to give a more precise hit-rate distribution and a recommended prefix normalization policy.

Happy to set up a short technical workshop next week.

—Marcus
